Actually, Albert Einstein won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921, but it was not specifically for his theory of relativity. The Nobel committee awarded him the prize "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect." The photoelectric effect was a pivotal discovery that helped establish the quantum nature of light and played a crucial role in the development of quantum theory.

While Einstein's theory of relativity is one of his most famous contributions to science, it was not the primary reason cited by the Nobel committee for his award. The theory of relativity, which includes both special relativity (published in 1905) and general relativity (published in 1915), revolutionized our understanding of space, time, and gravity, but it was not directly recognized by the Nobel Prize.
